questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted a destination where they spoke Spanish, and preferably in Central America. I also did not want to live in a big city.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My time in Mexico was varied, but overall I would say good, and I really enjoyed it and got exactly what I needed out of it. Most of the experiences I hear about exchange is that it was completely amazing, an unforgettable, life-changing experience, with friends for life, and I unfortunately did not have that. I was a lot older than most of the exchange students (28 vs. 22-ish), and I do not drink or take drugs or party. That limited me a lot in making friends, and so I didn't really have any the entire time I was there. I found everything to really be centered around partying, so like the trips that were organized are a little bit of culture, and a little bit of partying, you can't really take the partying part away (I asked). A lot of people live together, and I lived alone, which also made it hard to make friends. I have a lot of food allergies, so I found it really hard to find places to eat, and I couldn't go around and sample all the cuisine. I don't regret my exchange, but It just wasn't as good as I could've hoped. However, towards the end, I decided to go to the Yucatan peninsula and be near the sea and that was a lot better. It was amazing to just be in Mexico, and be finished with school, without the pressure of forced interaction. It was here that I felt my Spanish improved the most, because I had to use my Spanish a lot getting around. Between the exchange students, we mostly spoke English.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was fine. The International Office is extremely easy to get in touch with, they are available practically every day, all day, and you can even get a virtual appointment with them if needed.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I went to the International Office in person a couple of times to arrange my courses, that was pretty straightforward and easy. The Amigos Internacionales were also pretty helpful, we had a Whatsapp group with everyone (arranged at the online orientation, so don't miss that) and it was easy to ask questions in that group and get answers. There's also an in-person orientation once you arrive, and then you get a personal appointment with someone from the office to arrange everything, and they make sure everything is fine with your entry forms, student card, courses etc., so that was great. You get this time at the in-person orientation, so don't miss orientation!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Although the International Office is easy to get in touch with, to get them to actually do something is a little more difficult. They often promise they will do things, or send things, or contact people, but then don't do it, or don't get back to you. You have to follow up with them multiple times, but I think that might be part of the culture, and part of the whole experience :). It didn't bother me that much, the whole orientation process is extremely straightforward and they explain it to you multiple times.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It is so extremely easy to find a place to live. If I had to rate it out of 10, 10 being the easiest, I would rate it an 11. Cholula is just teeming with places to rent. I think it's nice to wait to find housing until you're actually in Cholula, because then you can see which neighbourhoods/areas you like, and maybe even hear other people's experiences of the houses. But I have no idea if the international houses fill up quickly. There's a lot, so I really think you'll always find a place, but I think it's nice to get a feel for Cholula first. Recommendations I guess are Casa Roja, Cholula Capital, Travel's Life, Charro Housing, Si Señor, etc. Those are international student houses that also sometimes organize parties or trips. It seems like most people live in such a house, and are very happy about it. There are probably more, but as I didn't live in them, I wouldn't know. I found my own place online, in Facebook groups such as “Renta de Casas y Departamentos Cholula,San Andrés y sus alrededores” and “rentas ventas zona UDLAP”. It's just so easy to find a place, I just put up a post with one sentence saying I was looking for a place for one person, and I got bombarded with 20+ offers of places to live. You could also just walk through Cholula, and look at all the places that say “renta”. Your Spanish has to be pretty good for this to work though I think, they will most likely want to communicate with you via Whatsapp in Spanish, and some might even send voice messages, so you obviously should be able to understand those. Obviously ask to tour the place before you rent it as well. I also recommend living in San Andrés, rather than San Pedro, although I did live in San Pedro (just on the other side of the pyramid, as close to San Andrés as possible), and I rather enjoyed it, because I got to bike through San Andrés every day to get to school. Most people wouldn't consider living farther away than walking distance though. Oh, and if you're sensitive about noise, stay away from la 14, that's the party street! In general though, Cholula is incredibly loud so I think it's very hard to actually find a truly quiet place, and there are lots of restaurants that may play music late. All in all though, even though I was a bit isolated because I didn't live in such a house, I was extremely happy with my one bedroom apartment, and I wasn't the only one living alone. I also heard some people had luck finding apartments on airbnb, but I found that way too expensive, even trying to negotiate a lower price. My budget was 8000 pesos, and I'm happy to say I found my amazing place for 7500 pesos.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I would recommend asking how permanent your contract is, or how it would work if you want to get out of it. I only heard of two cases, but some people didn't like the place they were staying at, and then wanted to move. Luckily, one person was easily able to terminate her contract and move, but the other one was kinda stuck which was too bad. The other thing is that Cholula is extremely loud, there are routinely like firework type things that sound more like gunshots or even cannon fire. It's kinda hard to avoid that, but if it matters to you, you could ask how noisy it gets at the place you will stay at. Also if it's close or not to the party street, maybe if you love partying you want that, or if you want some peace and quiet, live a little bit farther away from la 14.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Like I said, it's extremely easy to find a place. It was pretty loud at my place, since I lived so close to the pyramid and other churches (again, kinda hard to avoid), + I lived next to a restaurant that had live music every night until 12. But I had the whole apartment to myself (which was extremely important to me) living room, kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, it had common outdoor green areas (which I thought was amazing on the sunny days!), and the price even included cleaning twice (!!) a week + a change of towels and bed sheets once a week. Pretty luxury if you ask me ;).

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Hm, I mean the actual course registration is pretty easy, they send you a form via email, you fill it in, and send it back to them. What's difficult is finding information about the actual courses you want to take.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
1) they send you an old course catalogue during the summer, it's like an excel sheet with hundreds of courses.
2) you should look through this course catalogue and highlight which courses you're interested in (side note: it's kinda hard to figure out if you're interested in the courses or not, as you will only get the name of the course, and which faculty and program it's from. To get the (albeit quite short) course descriptions, you have to go the udlap website (
udlap.mx
), go to “oferta académica” (or just do it in English “schools”), find and click on the faculty (escuela) of the course. Once you get to this page, on the right hand side there should be like quadrants with program names on it, it's kinda like square pictures?? It's not intuitive at all lol, but find the study program the course is from, click on it, then scroll down to find “plan de estudios”, click it, scroll down until you see “periodos” with numbers underneath it. Those numbers correspond to semesters, so you might not know which semester the course you're interested in is from, so click through them until you find the course you're interested in. You could ofc, also do it the other way, as in find a study program you're interested, say anthropology, and then click through those semesters to find anthropology courses you could be interested in.
3) after you find which courses you're interested in, keep that safe until they send you the actual course catalogue. The actual course catalogue is not an excel sheet, but a search function on the website, it looks like this (
https://online.udlap.mx/inscripciones/catalogocursos.aspx?sesion=1
). That one is for fall 2022 though, so try (
https://online.udlap.mx/inscripciones/
) and scroll down almost until the end, until you find a section on the left that says “catálogo de cursos” and underneath, something like “otoño II trimestral 2022” “otoño II trimestral educación a distancia 2022” “otoño semestral 2022”. It will be trimestral for master's students, and semestral for bachelor's students. Click the appropriate one, and it'll bring you to the real course catalogue, which is a search function, where you can search for courses based on course number, course name, or professor.
Unfortunately this real course catalogue could be radically different than the one they sent you. For example, I picked around 50 courses I was initially interested in, but when they sent the actual one, only about 7 out of those 50 were offered. Yeah, not ideal. Apparently sometimes they switch around which semester courses are offered in. Anyways, obviously once you have the real course catalogue, repeat the process of finding courses you want, until you have 5. It might be a good idea to have a few back-ups, but as international students get to pick courses first, it's highly likely you'll get all the courses you want (unless you pick courses outside of your study area).
4) they will send you via email the course sign up form, so fill that in, and send it back to the international office (it will ask for like course name, course code, professor, course schedule, etc. all of that information which can be found in the actual course catalogue).
5) they will then send you back which courses you got, and if you want to change that, they have a separate add/drop form which you fill in and send back at specific times, like between 8 – 2. It can be a bit tricky though because it's all changed in real time. You may fill out the add form at 9 AM, but maybe someone sent one in at 8 AM and they got the last spot and not you. Or idk, sometimes it's just hard to keep up with if a class is full or not, but it should state it in the course catalogue.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Well the International Office at UDLAP can help you, but I got most help from the whatsapp group. Tbh, I didn't actually find the International Office to be that helpful regarding this process, maybe because they're so used to this system, it's hard for them to understand that it's actually kind of complicated. They're helpful about adding and dropping courses though, like in person, even though you're technically supposed to do it with the form.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Well. I was extremely unlucky in that out of the 50 (!!) courses I could be interested in, only about 7 were available after all. Out of those 7, about 5 overlapped each other with time, and you're not allowed to have overlapping classes, as attendance is mandatory. So. I spent an inordinate amount of time trying to figure everything out, but once I did, I got 4/5 of the courses I wanted. They didn't give me the last course because it was a marketing course and they said I didn't have any prior experience and so I wasn't allowed. So, try to pick courses you have some prior experience in, so this doesn't happen. There's unfortunately no way to know if they require previous experience though unless you email the teachers, and even then it might be difficult. I got written permission from the marketing course professor that I was allowed to take the course, and the International Office still didn't allow me to take it.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you're a Master's student, apply as a bachelor's. Apply normally to KU, but once you're nominated by KU, when you have to apply to UDLAP, check the box that says you want to take bachelor/undergraduate courses. KU will approve them as master's courses, if they're 4th year courses. That way, you have a MUCH bigger variety of courses to choose from, as the courses for Master's are extremely limited. Furthermore, courses that say they're in English may actually be in Spanish. Some professors are kind and say you can just speak English, especially if it's like a language class, but some expect you to only speak Spanish, even if it was supposed to be a course in English. Once again, there's really no way to tell, unless maybe you email the professor beforehand.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I had a very low expectation of the academic level at UDLAP, due to these evaluations, but I was pretty surprised to find that it was fine. It is structured a bit differently, but I really think it depends on the courses. Like, I know some people had midterms for example, but I didn't have any midterms. Some courses had like a small quiz every week, some courses had like 2 or 3 group essays during the semester, and for one course we had no course work during the semester, just class and regular homework, and one final exam that counted for 70%!

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I found all my professors to be extremely competent and knowledgable about their subject. All were engaging and interesting to learn from. The level was maybe a bit lower than I was used to, but there was DEFINITELY enough homework to do, and I was taking 4th year bachelor courses, as a Master's student. I thought it was extremely fine, and very academically sound.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They put a lot of emphasis on participating/speaking in class. I think for all of my classes, a percentage of the grade actually depends on it. I had one professor that would specifically ask every single person in the class for opinions on the text, so there's no way out.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Literaturas Prehispánicas
Etnología Histórica
Anthropological Studies of Conflicts
Literatura Mexicana Moderna
Temas Selectos 2

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I recommend Literaturas Prehispánicas, and Etnología Histórica because they were super interesting and gave me insight into Mexico, both pre-hispanic and contemporary or modern. Literaturas Prehispánicas is a must if you're interested in ancient cultures, like Mayan, Incan, Aztec, Olmec etc., and Etnología Histórica had the most amazing teacher Laura Romano, anything by her I recommend. She's so knowledgeable and talked about the construct of race, gender, etc. although, if you already know a lot about these topics, maybe it's not so interesting, as I felt like the things she said were interesting, but pretty “beginner”. I recommend Literatura Mexicana Moderna if you're interested in the Mexican revolution or war in general, but be prepared for a lot of reading (although it comes in cycles, like “read this book – let's discuss it for 2 weeks” aka, for those two weeks of discussion, you don't have any homework since you've already read the book). Martin Larsson is Swedish, very organized, and a good teacher.

questions.question: Insurance DKK *
Housing DKK per month *
Books DKK per month *
Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *
Communication (phone, internet, etc.) DKK per month *
Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: An extra statement from your doctor in Denmark before departure. They give you a form to fill out during the application process, that you need your doctor to sign, but then you also need an actual lægeerklæring in addition to that.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Some food was way more expensive than I expected. I can't eat gluten, so I was ofc happy to find gluten free pasta at all, but it cost more than x3 as much than in Denmark. I bought a lot of organic groceries, which I knew would be expensive, but it was still more expensive than I thought. I ordered food a lot, so it got expensive, but for me, it was 100% worth it.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There's both like extracurricular sports or classes like painting, photography, dance, music/singing lessons, personal defense classes, etc. which you have to pay for (talleres), and then there are also like academic “clubs” (organizaciones estudiantiles) which are free, which are more like “chess club”, “lgbtqia+ club”, “environmental club”, “science club” etc. but some of them were also like “flag football club”. I didn't want to pay so I didn't join the paid ones, plus I found it hard to reconcile them with my schedule, but I joined a couple of the free academic clubs, and I really recommend that, especially to meet other Mexicans. You can drop it after a few times, but if you go the first few, you can be in the whatsapp group, get invited to events, and possibly make friends that you can obviously keep, even if you stop coming to the meetings.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Mexico City, Teotihuacán, Cholula pyramid ofc, Puebla City, MUSEUMS!!! Go to all the museums you can, there's one next to the pyramid in Cholula and it was amazing! Botanical gardens in Cholula. visiting small cafés in Cholula.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: pretty easy

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: hmm no, as this was pretty hard for me as well. well, join international forum. maybe join more clubs and stuff? try to meet up with the amigos internacionales?

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The service-minded attitude. It seemed like in “service” situations, people were focused on giving me everything I wanted, and weren't concerned about their own needs, which I didn't appreciate. For example, when touring apartments to live in, landlords would often ask me when I would want to come and see it, and my response would always be “when does it fit you? What time is best for you? Is there something that you would you prefer?” because of course, I had all the time in the world, and I thought they would perhaps be busy, or have some preference, like maybe they're touring the same apartment at 1, so it would make sense for me to come directly before or after. But they seemed very annoyed at this attitude, and finally just ordered me to tell them what time I would come. It was the same with the cleaning lady or handymen, sometimes they would ask what time I would want them to come, and I would just say oh whenever suits you best, I'm home all day, because ofc they are busy and have their own lives etc. but that just seemed to confuse them, and make them upset so I had to learn to be kind of bossy, and be like “I want you to come here and clean/fix it at 2pm” or like “I am coming at 1 to tour the apartment”, even though I really didn't like it and never really got the hang of it to be honest. Also tipping! I consistently forgot to tip and often went back the next day to give them their tip. I always tipped 20%, unless they really didn't do anything at all, then 15%.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Everybody embraces lateness! That was so wonderful, I could take my time with everything, and know people weren't going to get annoyed or angry if I was late, and if I wasn't ready for someone to come over, I knew it didn't matter, because they were likely to come later anyways. So much less stress!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1) Cholula is extremely loud. Be prepared to experience gunshot-like noises (like fireworks, but much louder) pretty regularly, as well as what sounds like small explosions. 

2) Get Revolut. I don't know exactly how much I saved using Revolut, but given the exorbitant fees I know some other students were paying, like when withdrawing or transferring, I'm 100% satisfied. 

3) Don't use the water for cooking. I think most people know not to drink it, but a lot of exchange students were making pasta or rice or beans with the water. They thought it would be okay because they boiled it, but Mexicans told us this is EXTREMELY discouraged by everyone, and they would never do that. (I don't know if anybody got sick from doing that, but if Mexicans don't do it themselves, and warn us straight out not to do it, I'm not going to do it).

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Yes, if you want, maybe visit the campus before your classes start. The campus is huge, and if I hadn't gone there beforehand to figure out where all my classes were, I would've been extremely late to every single one because I would've been lost. They do give you a tour at orientation, but I got much more out of figuring it out myself, than from that. I still found the orientation tour useful though, as you could ask questions, and see things I wouldn't have known to look for myself. The guards are super nice, just tell them you're a new exchange student and have your student number ready to give them. 

I personally benefitted from coming 1.5 weeks before classes started and I wish I had had more time, like at least two weeks. Then I could've spent one week just acclimatizing and finding housing, and then one week of like “vacation” and rest before school started. They recommend you to come august 1st and even sometimes offer the amigos internacionales in the airport to help you get to Puebla, but that's just a waste of time. It's super easy to find the bus to Puebla, it's literally in the airport (or like, just outside, attached to it), and you can't really go wrong. You're looking for the bus to Paseo Destino, and then you just take an Uber or Didi to Cholula, super easy. I stayed in an Airbnb while looking for housing, 10/10 recommend.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer:
improving my spanish, the blissful warmth and sunshine during the so called “cold” months, meeting wonderful people (sadly none of them were students, but what can you do!), and the group tour i booked to Teotihuacan! simply amazing. I used
https://pueblatours.mx/tour-puebla-teotihuacan.html
, highly recommend, see if you can get Daniel Lima, and remember to tip!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding food I could eat. For some reason, a lot of the food I bought at the small tiendas or market went bad/mouldy within 2 – 3 days and that was really unappetizing to me. I had a really hard time finding fresh food at all actually, most small tiendas/kiosks don't have fresh food. But maybe that was just in San Pedro, as I noticed San Andrés had more. and eventually I figured out to take a didi to the supermarket, and that worked much better for me. I guess the greatest challenge was starting all over again. I had to figure out where to buy food (especially food I could eat!), where and how to buy water (and how to get it delivered), where to buy a pump for that water jug, how and where to find housing, how to pay my rent, how to get pesos, i could go on, just everything from scratch 'cause everything is new. But I learned, and had a great time! I enjoy being challenged, I think it makes you grow and that was one of my goals for this exchange which I am happy to say I achieved. I also unfortunately struggled with my mental health, and it was hard to find resources to help me, especially in English.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Yes, I think my experience and the struggles that I had are very particular to me, and not very applicable to the “typical” exchange student. I think most people are only happy to go to bars or clubs to meet up with people, and happy to go partying, and happy to live with other people, and therefore it will be very easy to make friends. Nevertheless, even though I only made two friends near the end of my trip (who weren't even students or Mexican), I still had a good time, and I definitely recommend it. As a side note, I also felt kind of obligated to see other parts of Mexico, and due to my mental health struggles I didn't get to see much outside of Puebla while I was in Cholula. For that reason, I went to Playa del Carmen for a few weeks, once school was over, just to see something else and get beach time in. But for me personally, this was a mistake, because all the challenges I just listed above, I had given myself again. I once again had to re-establish myself somewhere, and a few weeks just wasn't enough time. I'm sure for some people it works to backpack around or however they choose to travel, I just want to share an alternative opinion, that if I could have changed what I did, I would have 100% stayed in Cholula, and been there for 6 full months, instead of only 4.5 months. All my exams were over by December 10th.

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
